definition: Elucidate means to shed light on something murky until it makes sense.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word elucidate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know elucidate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A good guide can elucidate a cathedral ceiling in five sentences, and you spend the rest of the visit looking up.
Describe sits two steps below elucidate — describing only lays out what a thing looks like and where its parts sit, no why required, while to elucidate is to make the confusing finally make sense.
Explain stops short of elucidate — it offers the how and why, but to elucidate is to turn the lights on in a room people had given up on.

To clarify is the everyday verb for making something clear — restate it, define a term, sort out a mix-up. To elucidate promises the same result at a higher pitch: patient light shed on something genuinely murky. You clarify a scheduling email; a scholar elucidates a difficult poem.

To unpack is to open an idea up piece by piece — informal and hands-on, one part at a time. To elucidate aims at the finish line: the murky thing finally understood. You can unpack a paragraph for ten minutes and still leave it foggy; to elucidate it is to leave it lit.

To interpret is to say what something means — a poem, a contract clause, a strange result — often choosing among possible readings. To elucidate is to make the murky thing itself so plain that its meaning stops being in dispute. Interpreting offers a reading; elucidating turns on the light.

For years, Dena Okafor's editor forbade the phrase 'black hole' in headlines — readers, surveys said, skipped anything with it.
Okafor took the ban as a dare.
Her March column set out to elucidate the thing itself: not to dazzle, but to leave the reader holding a clear idea where a blur had been.
She spent four paragraphs on one image — a river narrowing to a waterfall — and never used an equation.
Letters arrived for a month.
A retired plumber wrote that he had read about these objects for forty years and understood them for the first time on a Tuesday.
The editor lifted the ban.
